1.title: instant karma?
1.hook: the vending machine tips over, everyone says karma: what the Buddha actually meant
1.carry: I am the owner of my actions
1.howItsDone: Buddhists understand karma as intentional action and what it ripens into; in many temples and monasteries a daily reflection is chanted that ends 'I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions', and people try to act from kind intentions in ordinary life.

segments.voice: Instant karma. A man kicks a vending machine and it tips over onto him. Someone cuts the line and their coffee comes out wrong. Everyone in the comments reaches for the same word, and they mean payback: the universe as a referee, settling scores where you can watch. It's satisfying. It's also not what the Buddha meant, and his version points the other way: back at the one acting. First, a guess.

Karma, or kamma in Pali, means action. A deed. Something done. Then the Buddha sharpened it. In one discourse he says it plainly: intention is what I call karma. Before the hand moves or the words come out, there's a leaning, a choice. That's where it starts. And then it grows. The old texts use a farming picture: deeds are seeds, and their results ripen like fruit. Not because a judge is keeping score. Because that's what seeds do. Two surprises. First, it's mostly about the one acting. Every choice shapes the chooser: patience, practiced, makes a patient person. Second, not everything is karma. Asked whether everything a person feels comes from past deeds, the Buddha said no: illness, weather, accidents and other people's choices play their part. So 'they deserved it' was never the point. In many temples and monasteries, people chant a reflection on it: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION` · `INTENTION IS KARMA` · `SEEDS, THEN FRUIT` · `NOT EVERYTHING IS KARMA` · then, large: `I AM THE OWNER OF MY ACTIONS.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind the next thing you'll do: a message, a meeting, a meal. Breathe in, and notice the intention underneath it. Breathe out, and let it lean toward kindness, if you like. That leaning is where karma starts.
Karma. Action, and the intention inside it: what you mean, and what it grows. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line: I am the owner of my actions. Not a weight to carry. A handle you can hold. See you tomorrow.

story.title: the insult nobody took
story.text: A furious man storms up to the Buddha and insults him to his face, again and again. The Buddha waits until he's finished. Then he asks: when guests come to your house and don't eat the food you offer, whose food is it? Mine, the man says. Then this abuse is yours too, the Buddha says: I don't accept it. The story says the man was so struck that he asked to become a monk himself.

2.title: why bow three times?
2.hook: palms together, forehead to the floor, three times: who the bows are for, and why the incense
2.carry: bow to what wakes you up
2.howItsDone: At a temple or home shrine, many Buddhists bow three times, palms together, often touching knees, hands and forehead to the floor, to the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha; many light incense and recite the three refuges, Buddham saranam gacchami, before chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, intention and what it grows. Today, a question a lot of people have at the altar: what am I doing when I bow?

Shoes off at the door. Palms together. Then down: knees, hands, forehead to the floor. Up. Again. And a third time. If you grew up going to temple, your body may know this before your mind ever asked why. Seen from outside, in a film or a yoga studio, it can look like worshiping a statue. It isn't quite that. The clue is the number three.
screen: `PALMS TOGETHER. FOREHEAD DOWN.` → `ONCE, TWICE, THREE TIMES.` → `WHY THREE?`

segments.voice: Each bow has a name, and together Buddhists call them the three jewels. The first is the Buddha: not a god, but a person who woke up. Many teachers say the bow is to that possibility of waking up, in anyone. The second is the Dharma, Dhamma in Pali: the teaching, and the way things actually are. The third is the Sangha: the community that practices it, monks and nuns, and in many places everyone walking the path together. Before chanting, many Buddhists say they go for refuge to these three, in Pali: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge, and so on for the other two. So the statue is a reminder, a bit like a photo of someone you love. And the incense? At a Buddhist altar it's offered as respect, not as something a god needs. One old verse says the scent of flowers only travels with the wind, but the goodness of a person travels even against it.

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring your palms together at your chest, if you like. Breathe in. As you breathe out, tip your head forward, just slightly: a small bow to whatever in you is trying to wake up.
The three jewels. The Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha: the one who woke up, the teaching, and the people who walk it. Second word.
Your line: bow to what wakes you up. Three bows, and none of them is to a statue. Day two, done.

story.title: the monk who bowed to everyone
story.text: A monk makes a whole town furious with one strange habit. He bows to everyone he meets, monks, nuns, strangers in the street, and tells each one: I would never look down on you, because you will become a buddha. People curse him. Some throw sticks and stones. He runs a little way off, turns around, and bows again from a safer distance. The story says he kept it up his whole life, and that he was the Buddha himself, in an earlier life.

3.title: is meditation Buddhist?
3.hook: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word: the old word underneath the apps
3.howItsDone: Buddhists practice sati in sitting meditation, in walking and in daily tasks, often following the four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind and mental patterns; in the tradition it is one part of the eightfold path, alongside ethical speech, action and livelihood.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three jewels, three bows to what wakes you up. Today, the question a lot of people with a meditation app quietly wonder.

Mindfulness is on water bottles, on coloring books, in the employee handbook somewhere between the dental plan and the parking policy. Meditation apps teach it, and some give old Buddhist practices new names along the way: insight meditation, calming meditation. So, is meditation Buddhist? Much of what the apps teach grew out of Buddhist practice. The longer answer starts with the old word underneath, and it turns out to be about remembering.
screen: `MINDFULNESS: ON A WATER BOTTLE.` → `NEW NAMES, OLD PRACTICES.` → `IS IT BUDDHIST?`

segments.voice: The old word is sati, in Pali. A Victorian scholar picked mindfulness to translate it, and the English stuck. Sati is related to a Sanskrit word for memory, so it isn't only paying attention. It's remembering to pay attention, and not letting it slip. The old texts give it a job. A fortress on the frontier has a wise gatekeeper who keeps out strangers and lets in the people he knows. He can only do that if he stays at his post and looks at every face. That gatekeeper, the text says, is sati. Here's what the apps often leave out. In the Buddha's teaching, mindfulness is one part of an eight-part path, sitting beside how you speak, how you act and how you earn a living. It isn't a productivity tool. It's meant to notice everything, even whether what you're doing is kind. So if you already sit with an app, you're practicing something with deep roots. And nobody has to become a Buddhist to sit: the tradition's own word for its teaching is an invitation, come and see. The tradition just sets it in a bigger room.
screen: `SATI — REMEMBERING TO NOTICE` · `THE GATEKEEPER AT THE GATE` · `ONE PART OF AN EIGHT-PART PATH` · `DEEP ROOTS, A BIGGER ROOM` · then, large: `REMEMBER TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest your attention on the breath. When a thought walks up to the gate, and one will, don't chase it and don't slam the gate. Just notice it: thought. Then remember the breath. Each time you remember, that's sati.
Sati. Mindfulness, older and fuller: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper at the gate. Third word on your strand.
Your line: remember to notice. Forgetting isn't failing; remembering again is the practice. Day three.

The bowl of oil, he says, is mindfulness of the body.

4.title: four truths, no jargon
4.hook: not a gloomy poster: a doctor's visit in four steps
4.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching; in Theravada countries the first sermon is remembered each year on the full moon of Asalha, and teachers in every school return to the four truths as the frame for practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sati, remembering to notice, one part of an eight-part path. Today, the teaching that path belongs to.

Buddhism has a reputation for being gloomy. Life is suffering, says the poster. But the first thing the Buddha is remembered teaching after he woke up sounds less like a poster and more like a visit to a good doctor. Here's what's wrong. Here's why. It can get better. Here's how. Four steps, in plain words.
screen: `LIFE IS SUFFERING?` → `MORE LIKE A DOCTOR'S VISIT.` → `FOUR STEPS.`

segments.voice: After he woke up, the story says, the Buddha walked to a deer park near Varanasi to find five old friends. What he told them came in four parts, called the four noble truths. One: there is dukkha. It's usually translated suffering, but it's wider: the ache of loss, of change, of things not quite fitting. Aging, sickness, death, being apart from what you love, not getting what you want. You could write the list yourself. Two: it has a cause, and the cause is craving, a thirst for things to be other than they are. Craving isn't love; it's the clutch inside wanting. Three: it can end. When the thirst lets go, the ache goes with it. The name for that ending is nirvana. Four: there's a path, with eight parts, from how you see things to how you speak, act, work and pay attention. Later teachers compared the four to a doctor: diagnosis, cause, cure, treatment. And the first one isn't a verdict. It doesn't say life is bad, or that you're doing it wrong. It says: this is hard, for everyone. Then it gets to work.
screen: `THERE IS DUKKHA` · `IT HAS A CAUSE: CRAVING` · `IT CAN END` · `THERE'S A PATH` · then, large: `A DIAGNOSIS, NOT A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, let something that's been hard lately come to mind, whatever comes. On the second, picture how many other people are carrying something like it today. On the third, let that land: not as a problem solved, but as company.
The four noble truths. There is dukkha; it has a cause; it can end; there's a path. Fourth word.
Your line: a diagnosis, not a verdict. It's not just you, and it's not the end of the story. See you tomorrow.

story.title: the poisoned arrow
story.text: A man is hit by a poisoned arrow. His friends bring a surgeon, but the man won't let him touch it until someone tells him who shot it: his name, his family, whether he was tall or short, what the bow was made of. He would die, the Buddha says, long before he got his answers. He told this to a monk who threatened to leave unless he got answers to the biggest questions about the universe. The Buddha's reply: I teach what helps. Dukkha, its cause, its end, and the path.

5.title: why monks don't beg
5.hook: a shaved head, a simple robe, a bowl at dawn: what the alms round really is
5.howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food, robes and medicine to monks and nuns, most visibly on the morning alms round in Theravada countries and at temple meals (in Sri Lanka, families 'give a dana'), and by giving to others in daily life; some meditation teachers teach freely on a dana basis.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four noble truths, a diagnosis, not a verdict. Today, the people who give their whole lives to the fourth one.

Dawn in a town in Thailand or Laos. A line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot down the street, heads shaved, each carrying a covered bowl. People kneel on mats by the curb with pots of rice. The monks don't ask for anything. And the people giving are often the ones who bow. To an outsider it can look like begging. It isn't, and the difference is today's word.
screen: `DAWN. A LINE OF MONKS.` → `THEY DON'T ASK.` → `THE GIVERS BOW.`

segments.voice: Dana means giving. Start with the monks. The shaved head and the simple robe go back to the Buddha's own leaving home: the story says he cut off his hair with his sword. Shaving it lets go of vanity, a way of saying: I'm not dressing for anyone. Traditionally a monk owns almost nothing: robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a few small things. In the Theravada tradition, monks don't eat after midday. That's a training rule for monastics, not a fast everyone keeps. And their food comes from giving. So the alms round isn't begging; it's an exchange. The monk gets a meal. The giver practices dana, which many Buddhists understand as making merit: good karma, and a lighter heart. When the Buddha met people who'd never heard him teach, the texts say he often started with giving, before anything else. In many East Asian monasteries, monks and nuns cook and farm for themselves, and lay people give in other ways. The open hand is the same.
screen: `THE SHAVED HEAD, THE SIMPLE ROBE` · `A BOWL, A RAZOR, A NEEDLE` · `NOTHING AFTER MIDDAY` · `NOT BEGGING: GIVING` · then, large: `GIVE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. On the first breath, notice what an open hand feels like. On the second, think of one thing you could give that isn't money: time, attention, a kind word. On the third, picture someone receiving it.
Dana. Giving: what fills the monk's bowl, and the first practice the Buddha taught. Fifth word.
Your line: give first. In the old order of teaching, the open hand came before everything else. That's day five.

screen: `DAY 5 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ONE FULL MOON, THREE STORIES.`

6.title: one full moon, three stories
6.hook: lanterns, a baby statue bathed in water, temples at dawn: the Buddha's birthday, and more
6.carry: he was a person who woke up
6.howItsDone: On Vesak, Buddhists in many Theravada countries visit temples, keep the precepts, give food, hang lanterns and remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and death together; in East Asia the Buddha's birthday is marked with lanterns and by pouring water or sweet tea over a statue of the infant Buddha, with his awakening and death remembered on other days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dana, giving, the open hand that fills the monk's bowl. Today, one full moon that means three things.

Lotus lanterns strung across a street in Seoul. A small statue of a baby, one hand pointing up, standing in a bowl of flowers while people line up to pour water over it. Families dressed in white at a temple in Sri Lanka before sunrise. Many of them will tell you it's the Buddha's birthday. Some will tell you it's more than that. Same festival, told differently. First, a guess.
screen: `LANTERNS. A BABY STATUE. WHITE CLOTHES.` → `THE BUDDHA'S BIRTHDAY?` → `AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Vesak takes its name from a spring month in the old Indian calendar. In many Theravada countries, like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, its full moon marks three things at once: the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his death. Tradition says all three fell on that same full moon. In Japan, the birthday has its own flower festival in April, and across much of East Asia his awakening and death are remembered on other days of the year. Different calendars, the same life. The water poured over the baby statue recalls a story: when he was born, streams of water fell from the sky to bathe him. And who is everyone celebrating? Buddha isn't a name. It's a title, from a word meaning to wake up. In one old story, a man follows his footprints and asks: are you a god? No. A spirit? No. A human being? No again. Then what are you? Remember me, he says, as awake. Not a god, by his own account: a person who woke up.
screen: `VESAK — A SPRING FULL MOON` · `BIRTH, AWAKENING, DEATH` · `DIFFERENT DAYS, SAME LIFE` · `BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP` · then, large: `HE WAS A PERSON WHO WOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture a single lantern being lit. On the second, bring to mind one person whose life lit something in yours. On the third, let yourself be glad they were here.
Vesak. One spring full moon for his birth, his awakening and his death, told differently in different places. Sixth word.
Your line: he was a person who woke up. That's who the lanterns are for. Day six, done.

story.title: the poor woman's lamp
story.text: The whole city is lighting lamps for the Buddha, the king's by the thousand, and a poor woman has a single coin. She spends it on a little oil, barely enough for one small lamp, and sets it down among the others. By morning every lamp has burned out except hers. One of the Buddha's great disciples tries to put it out, and it won't go out. The Buddha tells him to stop: that lamp was lit with a whole heart.
story.source: the poor woman's lamp, from the Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish; told at lantern festivals in Korea and elsewhere

7.title: what carries on?
7.hook: if there's no soul packed up and moved, what goes on? one flame lighting the next
7.howItsDone: Many Buddhists understand death as followed by rebirth shaped by karma, and mark a death with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites (in many communities over the following seven weeks); traditions describe the process differently, and some teachers also apply it to moment-to-moment experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vesak, and a person who woke up. Six words so far: karma, the three jewels, sati, the four noble truths, dana, Vesak. Today, the seventh.
screen: `KARMA · THE THREE JEWELS · SATI · THE FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS · DANA · VESAK`

segments.voice: When a grandparent dies, many Buddhist families do more than hold a funeral. Monks chant. Food is offered, and the good of it is dedicated to the one who died. In many East Asian and Tibetan communities, the prayers go on for forty-nine days, a time, those traditions say, between one life and the next. Behind it is the question day one left hanging: when a life ends, what happens to everything it set growing? And there's a twist. In the Buddha's teaching, no fixed soul packs up and moves.
screen: `A GRANDPARENT DIES.` → `FORTY-NINE DAYS OF PRAYERS.` → `WHAT GOES ON?`

segments.voice: Many Buddhist traditions teach rebirth: a life, when it ends, is followed by another, shaped by karma, round and round, until someone wakes up. Teachers often prefer the word rebirth to reincarnation, because nothing solid moves across. An old book of questions gives the best-known picture. A king asks a monk: is the one who's reborn the same person, or someone else? Neither, says the monk. Light one lamp from another. Did the flame move over? No. Is the new flame unrelated? No again: it was lit from the first. So what passes on is momentum, not a soul. Traditions describe the details very differently: how, where, how soon. Some teachers also point to a version anyone can watch: each moment lit from the last. If you're not sure about rebirth, you're not behind: plenty of Buddhists practice for years with that question still open. And for anyone unsure about all of it, there's an old answer too. The Buddha once spoke to villagers who didn't know which teachers to believe. A kind, clear life is good either way, he told them: if there's another life, it goes well; if there isn't, this one already does.
screen: `REBIRTH, NOT A SOUL MOVING HOUSE` · `SAME PERSON? NEITHER, NOR ANOTHER` · `ONE LAMP LIGHTS ANOTHER` · `GOOD EITHER WAY` · then, large: `ONE FLAME LIGHTS THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, notice this breath arriving. On the second, notice that it isn't the one before, and that it came from the one before. On the third, let it go, and let the next one light itself.
Rebirth. Not a soul moving house: one flame lighting the next, carried by karma. Seventh word, and a week's worth.
Your line: one flame lights the next. That's week one: seven words, from a meme to a lamp. Tomorrow, the word behind the first truth.

story.title: the king and the chariot
story.text: A king who has beaten every debater in his kingdom sits down across from a monk named Nagasena and asks his name. Nagasena, the monk says, but that's only a label: no fixed person is found behind it. The king pounces: then who am I talking to? The monk asks how the king came. By chariot. Is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The seat? No, no, no, says the king, it's the name for all the parts together. Exactly, says Nagasena.
story.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda) II.1.1

wrong.myth: Buddhist rebirth is a soul moving into a new body.
